propositions.text: The applicant is a Pakistani citizen who claimed refugee protection as a Shia Muslim fearing Sunni extremist persecution.
propositions.quote: The applicant is a citizen of Pakistan. He sought refugee protection in Canada on the basis that, as a Shia Muslim, he has a well-founded fear of persecution by Sunni extremists.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the claim on credibility grounds and because the applicant had an internal flight alternative in Islamabad.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) rejected the claim on credibility grounds and because, in any event, the applicant has an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Islamabad.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant, a Pakistani Shia Muslim fearing Sunni extremists, had his refugee claim rejected by the RPD on credibility and internal flight alternative grounds.

propositions.text: The RAD found a procedural fairness breach because the RPD relied on undisclosed POE notes and remedied it by disclosing notes and inviting submissions.
propositions.quote: The RAD agreed with the applicant that there had been a breach of procedural fairness because the RPD had relied on information in Port of Entry (POE) notes that had not been disclosed to the applicant. The RAD sought to remedy this breach by having the notes disclosed to the applicant and inviting submissions regarding the notes from the applicant.

propositions.text: On the merits, the RAD agreed with the RPD that the applicant failed to provide credible evidence to establish his claim.
propositions.quote: On the merits of the appeal, the RAD agreed with the RPD that the applicant had failed to provide sufficient credible evidence to establish his claim.

propositions.text: The RAD found it unnecessary to address the internal flight alternative issue as the credibility finding was determinative.
propositions.quote: The RAD further found that, since this was determinative of the appeal, it was not necessary to address the IFA issue.

propositions.text: The RAD dismissed the appeal and confirmed the RPD’s determination that the applicant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The RAD therefore dismissed the appeal and confirmed the RPD’s determination that the applicant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found procedural fairness breach but upheld the RPD's credibility finding, dismissed the appeal, and confirmed the applicant is not a refugee or protected person.

propositions.text: The applicant submits the RAD's handling of POE notes breached procedural fairness and that the decision is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: He submits that the manner in which the RAD dealt with the POE notes did not meet the requirements of procedural fairness. He also submits that the decision is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the RAD's handling of POE notes breached procedural fairness and that the decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: The court disagrees that the RAD's handling of POE notes was unfair and that the decision was unreasonable, so the judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: I do not agree that the manner in which the RAD dealt with the POE notes was unfair. Nor do I agree that the decision is unreasonable. This application for judicial review must, therefore, be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no unfairness or unreasonableness in the RAD's decision and dismisses the judicial review application.

propositions.text: The applicant was born in Mandi Bahauddin, Pakistan, in December 1983.
propositions.quote: The applicant was born in Mandi Bahauddin, Pakistan, in December 1983.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant was born in Mandi Bahauddin, Pakistan, in December 1983.

propositions.text: The applicant began as general secretary of a youth wing of an Imam Bargah in February 2017 and faced problems after a September 2018 inter-faith cricket match fight.
propositions.quote: According to his Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative, the applicant began serving as the general secretary of the youth wing of an Imam Bargah in Mandi Bahauddin in February 2017. The applicant claims that his problems began in September 2018, when he arranged an inter-faith cricket match with Sunni players. A fight broke out during the match.

propositions.text: After the match, Sunnis spread rumours and Sunni clerics made anti-Shia speeches against the applicant.
propositions.quote: after the match Sunnis started spreading rumours about him, alleging that he “took the side of the Shias.” The applicant claims that local Sunni clerics then became involved and began making anti-Shia speeches.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant says he faced hostility after a 2018 inter-faith cricket match, with rumours and anti-Shia speeches by Sunni clerics.

propositions.text: In October 2018, the applicant received threatening calls from Sipah-Sahaba members and reported to police who took no action.
propositions.quote: In October 2018, the applicant began receiving threatening phone calls from individuals claiming to belong to the Sipah-Sahaba (SSP), a fundamentalist Sunni group. The applicant claims he reported this to the police, but they did not take any action.

propositions.text: Fearing for safety, the applicant stopped working for the Imam Bargah.
propositions.quote: Fearing for his safety, the applicant stopped working for the Imam Bargah.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant received threats from a Sunni group in October 2018, reported to police who did nothing, and then stopped working for the Imam Bargah.

propositions.text: On November 18, 2018, the applicant was threatened by Lashkar-e-Jhangvi and reduced religious and social activities.
propositions.quote: On November 18, 2018, he received a call from someone claiming to belong to the Lashkar-e-Jhangvi (LeJ), another fundamentalist Sunni group. The caller threatened to kill the applicant because of his work in the Shia community. The applicant claims that, after receiving this call, he cut down on his religious and social activities and mostly stayed at home.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant was threatened by Lashkar-e-Jhangvi in November 2018 and reduced his religious and social activities.

propositions.text: A Sunni cleric issued a fatwa against the applicant on December 2, 2018, leading to a social boycott.
propositions.quote: On December 2, 2018, a Sunni cleric issued a fatwa against the applicant identifying him as an infidel. The applicant claims he suffered a “social boycott” in his community after the issuance of the fatwa.

propositions.text: The applicant submitted a copy of the fatwa to the RPD.
propositions.quote: The applicant submitted a copy of the fatwa to the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: A fatwa was issued against the applicant in December 2018 causing social boycott; he submitted the fatwa to the RPD.

propositions.text: The applicant obtained a US visitor visa on December 19, 2018.
propositions.quote: On December 19, 2018, the applicant obtained a US visitor visa.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant obtained a US visitor visa on December 19, 2018.

propositions.text: On December 24, 2018, a mob attacked the applicant’s home; police intervened and took a statement.
propositions.quote: On December 24, 2018, a mob attacked the applicant’s home. Neighbours intervened to stop the attack. The police attended and took a statement from the applicant.

propositions.text: After the attack, the applicant and family left Mandi Bahauddin for Multan and went into hiding.
propositions.quote: After this incident, the applicant, his wife, and their children left Mandi Bahauddin for the city of Multan and went into hiding there.

paragraphs.summary: A mob attacked the applicant’s home in December 2018; police took a statement and the family fled to Multan and hid.

propositions.text: The applicant left Pakistan for the US on December 29, 2018, and entered Canada irregularly on January 3, 2019, claiming refugee protection.
propositions.quote: The applicant left Pakistan for the United States on December 29, 2018. On January 3, 2019, he entered Canada irregularly at the Roxham Road border crossing and made a claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant left Pakistan for the US in December 2018 and entered Canada irregularly in January 2019 to claim refugee protection.

propositions.text: In 2019 and 2020, LeJ and SSP members burned the applicant’s home and searched his father’s home for him.
propositions.quote: On October 10, 2019, members of the LeJ and the SSP burned down the applicant’s home. On February 9, 2020, and again on November 17, 2020, members of the LeJ and the SSP attended the home of the applicant’s father looking for the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: LeJ and SSP members burned the applicant’s home in 2019 and searched his father’s home in 2020 for him.

propositions.text: The Minister alleged the applicant said to CBSA that he did not intend to come to Canada but fled US due to renewed threats.
propositions.quote: When interviewed by a Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officer after entering Canada, the applicant explained that it had not been his intention to come to Canada but, after arriving in the United States, he was informed that his agents of persecution had learned he was there and had threatened him again so he decided to seek refugee protection in Canada.

propositions.text: The applicant failed to disclose an unsuccessful 2017 US visa application predating his alleged problems.
propositions.quote: The applicant had failed to disclose to Canadian authorities that he had applied unsuccessfully for a US visitor visa in December 2017, before any of the problems he was alleging had occurred.

propositions.text: The applicant’s 2018 US visa application personal info materially differed from what he gave Canadian authorities.
propositions.quote: Personal information the applicant provided in connection with his 2018 US visa application (e.g. details of his education and employment) differed in material respects from what he provided to Canadian authorities in connection with his refugee claim.

propositions.text: The applicant’s Facebook page shows he lives in Toronto, Ontario.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s publicly available Facebook page indicates that he lives in Toronto, Ontario.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister alleged the applicant made inconsistent statements about US visa applications and residence, and did not disclose all relevant info.

propositions.text: The Minister provided biometric report, 2018 US visa application, and Facebook screenshot but no POE notes with the notice of intent to intervene.
propositions.quote: With the notice of intent to intervene, the Minister provided a Five Country Conference Biometric report regarding the applicant from the US Department of Homeland Security, a copy of the applicant’s 2018 US visa application, and a screenshot of the applicant’s Facebook page. The notice of intent to intervene refers to POE Examination Notes but no such notes were provided with the notice.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister submitted biometric report, visa application, and Facebook screenshot but no POE notes with the intervention notice.

propositions.text: The RPD hearing occurred on August 20, 2021, and the decision rejecting the claim was dated November 8, 2021.
propositions.quote: The hearing before the RPD took place on August 20, 2021. The RPD rejected the claim in a decision dated November 8, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD hearing was on August 20, 2021, and the claim was rejected in a November 8, 2021 decision.

propositions.text: The RPD had credibility concerns about the applicant for omitting his 2017 US visa application and inconsistent explanations.
propositions.quote: The applicant had stated in his BOC narrative that he obtained a US visitor visa on December 19, 2018, after the fatwa was issued.However, the applicant omitted any mention of his 2017 US visa application.The fact that the applicant had tried to obtain a US visa in 2017 suggested he was trying to leave Pakistan “even before any alleged risk.” The applicant’s failure to mention this suggests that he “was aware that the claim would be less compelling if [he] had a history of trying to leave Pakistan” so he attempted to conceal this fact.

propositions.text: The applicant gave inconsistent and vague explanations for false info in his 2018 US visa application.
propositions.quote: The applicant gave inconsistent and vague explanations for why false information was used in his 2018 US visa application.

propositions.text: The applicant omitted from his narrative that his persecutors learned he was in the US, a material omission.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s failure to include in his narrative the allegation that his agents of persecution had learned he was in the United States and that this was why he decided to go to Canada was a material omission.

propositions.text: The applicant’s Facebook disclosure of being in Canada despite alleged US threats suggests lack of subjective fear.
propositions.quote: The applicant disclosing on his Facebook page that he is in Canada despite allegedly having had to leave the United States because his agents of persecution had learned he was there suggests a lack of subjective fear on the part of the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found credibility issues due to omissions, inconsistent explanations, and Facebook posts undermining the applicant’s fear claim.

propositions.text: The applicant submitted affidavits, police reports, and a fatwa to corroborate his narrative.
propositions.quote: The applicant had provided a number of documents to corroborate his narrative: affidavits from various individuals confirming the events described by the applicant; police reports concerning attacks on the applicant and his home; and a copy of the fatwa.

propositions.text: The RPD found affidavits used similar language, unclear if affiants witnessed events, and were mostly from people close to the applicant.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the affidavits used similar language and that it was unclear whether the affiants had personally witnessed the events they described or had been told about them by the applicant. As well, most of the affidavits were “from people close to the [applicant].”

propositions.text: Country reports state fraudulent documents are readily available in Pakistan, so the RPD gave little weight to these documents.
propositions.quote: The RPD also noted that country conditions reports stated that fraudulent documents are readily available throughout Pakistan. For these reasons, the RPD found that the documents “have little probative weight” and did not overcome its credibility concerns.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the applicant’s supporting documents unpersuasive due to similarities, questionable witness credibility, and country conditions.

propositions.text: The RPD concluded the applicant was not attacked after the cricket match and LeJ/SSP did not track him to the US.
propositions.quote: Regarding the events underlying the claim, the RPD concluded that the applicant had not been attacked after organizing an inter-faith cricket match and that the LeJ/SSP did not track him to the United States.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the applicant was not attacked after the cricket match and was not tracked to the US by LeJ/SSP.

propositions.text: The RPD found the applicant lacks subjective fear of persecution and faces no risk from LeJ/SSP if returned to Pakistan.
propositions.quote: In summary, the RPD found that the applicant does not have a subjective fear of persecution at the hands of the LeJ/SSP in Pakistan, nor does he face a risk of harm from these groups should he return to Pakistan.

propositions.text: Alternatively, the RPD found the applicant had a viable internal flight alternative in Islamabad and rejected the claim.
propositions.quote: The RPD also found, in the alternative, that the applicant had a viable IFA in Islamabad. As a result, it rejected the claim for protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no subjective fear or risk from LeJ/SSP and that the applicant had a viable internal flight alternative, rejecting the claim.

propositions.text: There was a breach of procedural fairness because POE examination notes were relied on but not disclosed despite request.
propositions.quote: the applicant submitted that there had been a breach of the requirements of procedural fairness because the RPD had relied on information in the POE examination notes but those notes had not been disclosed to him despite his having requested them prior to the hearing.

propositions.text: The RPD's adverse credibility findings and assessment of documentary evidence were incorrect.
propositions.quote: He also challenged the correctness of the RPD’s adverse credibility findings as well as its assessment of the documentary evidence provided to corroborate his narrative.

propositions.text: The RPD erred in finding that he had a viable internal flight alternative (IFA).
propositions.quote: The applicant also argued that the RPD erred in finding that he had a viable IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argued procedural fairness was breached by nondisclosure of POE notes, challenged adverse credibility findings, and IFA finding.

propositions.text: Minister provided POE notes from CBSA officer's interview on January 8, 2019, describing applicant's reasons for refugee claim and threats.
propositions.quote: In response to a request from the RAD, on March 2, 2022, the Minister provided the notes taken by the Inland CBSA Officer who interviewed the applicant at the Montreal Urban Processing Centre on January 8, 2019.

propositions.text: Notes state applicant was threatened due to role in Shia Youth, fled to US, threatened again, then came to Canada.
propositions.quote: I asked Mr. AFZAL why he made a claim for refugee protection today. Stated that as he is involved with the Shia Youth...

paragraphs.summary: The Minister provided POE notes showing applicant's interview about threats and reasons for refugee claim.

propositions.text: RAD identified six credibility concerns not addressed by RPD and invited applicant's submissions, including on POE notes.
propositions.quote: On March 9, 2022, the RAD wrote to the applicant identifying six “credibility concerns” that were not addressed in the RPD’s reasons and inviting the applicant to provide submissions in response to the concerns.

propositions.text: One concern was omission of threats learned in US and fear of being located there from BOC narrative.
propositions.quote: Among these concerns was the omission from the BOC narrative of the threats the applicant learned about after arriving in the United States and his fear of being located there.

propositions.text: RAD invited submissions on Port of Entry Examination notes.
propositions.quote: The RAD also invited the applicant to make submissions “in relation to the Port of Entry Examination notes.”

paragraphs.summary: The RAD identified credibility concerns including omissions and invited submissions on POE notes.

propositions.text: Applicant's counsel responded addressing six credibility concerns and said omission of US fear was not misleading as it was told at port of entry.
propositions.quote: With respect to the POE notes in particular, he wrote: “[T]he only relevance I see is that it corroborates Mr. Afzal’s position...

propositions.text: Counsel stated no attempt to mislead or omit facts; fear in US was thought irrelevant to claim against Pakistan.
propositions.quote: There was no attempt to mislead or misinform or omit facts, it was just thought that it was not relevant to the present claim against Pakistan and besides he had already told immigration this.

propositions.text: Counsel suggested a re-hearing might be offered if concerns remain or new issues arise.
propositions.quote: If there are still concerns or my writing has raised other issues then perhaps a re-hearing could be offered to Mr. Afzal to better address these concerns.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's counsel responded to RAD's concerns, explained omissions, and suggested a re-hearing if needed.

propositions.text: RAD agreed with applicant that nondisclosure of POE notes breached procedural fairness at RPD.
propositions.quote: Looking first at the POE notes, the RAD agreed with the applicant that the Minister’s failure to disclose the notes had occasioned a breach of procedural fairness at the RPD.

propositions.text: RAD found breach was minor because Minister's intervention content matched POE notes.
propositions.quote: The RAD was satisfied, however, that this was a minor breach because “the content of the Minister’s intervention is consistent with the content of the POE Examination notes.”

propositions.text: Breach was remedied on appeal by disclosing notes and allowing submissions.
propositions.quote: The RAD was also satisfied that the breach had been remedied on appeal because the notes had been disclosed to the applicant and he was provided with an opportunity to address them in submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found nondisclosure breached fairness but was minor and remedied on appeal by disclosure and submissions.

propositions.text: RAD agreed with RPD's negative credibility assessment on appeal merits.
propositions.quote: On the merits of the appeal, the RAD largely agreed with the RPD’s negative assessment of the applicant’s credibility.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to explain omission of US threats from BOC narrative.
propositions.quote: The RAD found that the applicant had failed to provide a reasonable explanation for the omission of the threats he received in the United States from his BOC narrative.

propositions.text: Applicant's social media disclosure of location contradicted claim of fear in US.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s disclosure of his location on social media was inconsistent with his claim in the POE interview that he was fearful in the United States because he had been located there.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to mention 2017 US visa application without reasonable explanation, warranting negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s failure to mention his 2017 US visa application, for which the applicant had not provided a reasonable explanation, warranted a negative inference as to his credibility.

propositions.text: RAD agreed two affidavits were almost identical and unclear if affiants witnessed events.
propositions.quote: As for the applicant’s supporting evidence, the RAD agreed with the RPD that two of the affidavits were almost identical. The RAD also agreed that it is unclear whether the affiants personally witnessed the events they describe.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agreed with RPD's negative credibility findings and noted inconsistencies and affidavit issues.

propositions.text: RAD found supporting documents did not overcome credibility concerns including omissions and inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: I have reviewed the supporting documents submitted by the Appellant and find that they do not overcome the significant credibility concerns outlined above...

propositions.text: Applicant's explanations did not reasonably explain discrepancies and undermined credibility.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant’s explanations do not reasonably explain the discrepancies and that they undermine his credibility.

propositions.text: Applicant did not establish allegations on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, the allegations that form the basis of his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concluded applicant's evidence failed to overcome credibility concerns and did not prove allegations.

propositions.text: RAD dismissed appeal and confirmed RPD's decision applicant is neither Convention refugee nor person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The RAD therefore dismissed the appeal and confirmed the RPD’s decision that the applicant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismissed the appeal and confirmed the RPD's negative refugee and protection finding.

propositions.text: Applicant challenges procedural fairness of RAD's handling of POE notes and merits decision on appeal.
propositions.quote: The applicant challenges both the fairness of the procedure by which the RAD dealt with the POE examination notes as well as the decision on the merits of his appeal.

propositions.text: No dispute on judicial review approach to these issues.
propositions.quote: There is no dispute about how the Court should approach these issues on judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant challenges procedural fairness and merits decision; no dispute on judicial review approach.

propositions.text: Court must independently assess procedural fairness of decision maker's process using Baker factors and relevant case law.
propositions.quote: First, to determine whether the procedure followed by the RAD met the requirements of procedural fairness, the reviewing court must conduct its own analysis of the process the decision maker followed and determine for itself whether that process was fair having regard to all the relevant circumstances, including those identified in Baker v Canada...

propositions.text: This analysis is functionally correctness standard; no deference owed to RAD on procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: This is functionally the same as applying the correctness standard of review: see Canadian Pacific Railway Co at paras 49-56 and Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers v Canada...

propositions.text: Ultimate question is whether applicant knew case to meet and had full, fair chance to respond.
propositions.quote: The ultimate question “is whether the applicant knew the case to meet and had a full and fair chance to respond” (Canadian Pacific Railway Co at para 56).

propositions.text: Burden is on applicant to prove procedural fairness requirements not met.
propositions.quote: The burden is on the applicant to demonstrate that the requirements of procedural fairness were not met.

paragraphs.summary: Court independently assesses procedural fairness with no deference; burden on applicant to prove breach.

propositions.text: RAD's merits decision reviewed on reasonableness standard requiring coherent, rational, justified analysis.
propositions.quote: Second, the RAD’s decision on the merits of the appeal is reviewed on a reasonableness standard. A reasonable decision “is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov...

propositions.text: Reasonable decisions get deference; must have transparent, intelligible justification and no fatal flaws.
propositions.quote: A decision that displays these qualities is entitled to deference from the reviewing court (ibid.). For a decision to be reasonable, a reviewing court “must be able to trace the decision maker’s reasoning without encountering any fatal flaws in its overarching logic...

propositions.text: Decisions lacking transparent, intelligible justification are unreasonable.
propositions.quote: On the other hand, “where reasons are provided but they fail to provide a transparent and intelligible justification [. . .], the decision will be unreasonable” (Vavilov at para 136).

paragraphs.summary: RAD's merits decision reviewed for reasonableness requiring coherent, justified, transparent reasoning.

propositions.text: Court does not reweigh evidence or interfere with factual findings absent exceptional circumstances.
propositions.quote: When applying the reasonableness standard, it is not the role of the reviewing court to reweigh or reassess the evidence considered by the decision maker or to interfere with factual findings unless there are exceptional circumstances (Vavilov at para 125).

propositions.text: Reasonableness standard applies to evidence assessment and inferences including credibility findings.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, the test of reasonableness and its requirements of justification, intelligibility and transparency apply to an administrative decision maker’s assessment of the evidence and to the inferences the decision maker draws from that evidence (Kreishan v Canada...

propositions.text: Adverse credibility findings must be justified by evidence and reasons.
propositions.quote: Consequently, adverse findings of fact and or adverse inferences with respect to credibility must find their justification in the evidence before the decision maker and their expression in the decision maker’s reasons (ibid.).

paragraphs.summary: Court defers to factual findings but requires justification and transparency for adverse credibility findings.

propositions.text: Applicant must show RAD's decision is unreasonable with serious shortcomings lacking justification, intelligibility, transparency.
propositions.quote: The onus is on the applicant to demonstrate that the RAD’s decision is unreasonable. To set aside a decision on this basis, the reviewing court must be satisfied that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant bears burden to prove RAD's decision unreasonable due to serious shortcomings.

propositions.text: Disclosure of POE notes and submissions opportunity did not cure procedural fairness breach; worsened it.
propositions.quote: The applicant submits that the disclosure of the POE notes and the opportunity to address them in submissions did not cure the breach of procedural fairness in this case. On the contrary, this only exacerbated the breach of procedural fairness at the RPD because the applicant continued to be deprived of a meaningful opportunity to address a central piece of evidence.

propositions.text: RAD should have returned matter to RPD for new hearing.
propositions.quote: According to the applicant, the RAD should have returned the matter to the RPD for a new hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues disclosure and submissions did not cure breach and RAD should have ordered new hearing.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with applicant's submission on procedural fairness breach cure.
propositions.quote: I disagree.

paragraphs.summary: Court disagrees with applicant's argument that breach was not cured.

propositions.text: RAD's characterization of nondisclosure as minor breach is apt because notes' content matched Minister's intervention.
propositions.quote: I would begin by observing that the RAD’s characterization of the failure to disclose the POE notes as a “minor breach” of procedural fairness is entirely apt. As the RAD points out, the information in the notes was set out accurately in the Minister’s notice of intervention; the notes themselves did not contain any additional relevant information.

propositions.text: Applicant was aware of information and had full opportunity to respond at RPD despite nondisclosure of notes.
propositions.quote: As a result, even though he did not have the document from which the information the Minister relied on was obtained, he was aware of that information and had a full opportunity to respond to it at the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees breach was minor as applicant knew info and had full chance to respond despite nondisclosure.

propositions.text: Applicant had meaningful opportunity to address POE notes on appeal; notes added nothing new.
propositions.quote: In light of this, I am satisfied that the applicant had a meaningful opportunity to address the POE notes on appeal. In short, they added nothing new to the case the applicant already had a full opportunity to meet at the RPD.

propositions.text: Applicant's counsel had nothing new to say when given chance to submit on notes.
propositions.quote: It is noteworthy that, when given the opportunity to provide further submissions on the notes, his counsel had nothing new to say.

propositions.text: Applicant has not identified any additional information he was prevented from providing due to RAD's process.
propositions.quote: On review, the applicant has not identified any additional information he was prevented from providing because of the manner in which the RAD proceeded.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds applicant had meaningful chance to address notes and no new info was withheld.

propositions.text: RAD did not expressly address referral back to RPD or subsection 110(6) hearing requirement.
propositions.quote: The RAD does not expressly address the applicant’s request that the matter be referred back to the RPD for a new hearing. Nor does it expressly consider whether, having admitted the POE notes as new evidence, a hearing was warranted under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Despite lack of express consideration, process met procedural fairness as notes added nothing new.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, since the POE notes did not add anything new to the case the applicant had to meet, I am satisfied that the process followed by the RAD met the requirements of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes RAD did not address referral or hearing but process met fairness as notes added nothing new.

propositions.text: RAD's adverse credibility findings are unreasonable and RAD ignored substantial corroborating evidence.
propositions.quote: The applicant submits that the RAD’s decision is unreasonable because the RAD’s adverse credibility determinations do not stand up to scrutiny. He also submits that the RAD ignored a substantial body of evidence capable of corroborating the core elements of his claim, leaving a fundamental gap in the RAD’s analysis.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD's adverse credibility findings are unreasonable and ignored corroborating evidence.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with applicant's submission that RAD's decision is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Once again, I do not agree.

paragraphs.summary: Court disagrees that RAD's decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: The applicant challenged the RPD's adverse credibility findings and the IFA determination.
propositions.quote: In his appeal, the applicant challenged the RPD’s adverse credibility findings as well as the IFA determination.

propositions.text: The RAD did not find it necessary to address the IFA issue.
propositions.quote: As noted above, the RAD did not find it necessary to address the IFA issue.

propositions.text: The RPD erred by drawing adverse inferences from failure to mention US threats, social media disclosure, and failure to disclose 2017 US visa application.
propositions.quote: the applicant submitted that the RPD had erred in the following respects: (1) by drawing an adverse inference from the applicant’s failure to mention the threats he received in the United States in his BOC narrative; (2) by drawing an adverse inference from the applicant’s having disclosed his location on social media; and (3) by drawing an adverse inference from the applicant’s failure to disclose his 2017 US visa application.

propositions.text: The RPD erred in giving his supporting evidence little probative weight and finding it did not overcome credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The applicant also submitted that the RPD had erred in giving his supporting evidence “little probative weight” and in finding that the evidence did not overcome the credibility concerns it identified.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant challenges the RPD's adverse credibility findings and IFA determination, alleging errors in adverse inferences and weight given to evidence.

propositions.text: The applicant has not persuaded that the RAD's credibility determinations are unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the applicant has not persuaded me that any of them are unreasonable.

propositions.text: The RAD addressed each alleged error in detail and explained why it agreed with the RPD's findings.
propositions.quote: The RAD addressed in detail each of the errors the applicant had alleged. In transparent, intelligible, and justified reasons, it explained why it was not persuaded that the RPD had erred in any of the ways the applicant alleged and why it agreed with the RPD’s findings.

propositions.text: The applicant identified no fundamental flaws in the RAD's reasoning, only disagreement with conclusions.
propositions.quote: The applicant has not identified any fundamental flaws in the RAD’s reasoning. Rather, he simply disagrees with the RAD’s conclusions and urges me to do the same.

propositions.text: The Court's role on judicial review under reasonableness standard is not to substitute its own conclusions.
propositions.quote: that is not the role of the Court on judicial review on a reasonableness standard.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD's credibility determinations reasonable and declines to substitute its own conclusions on judicial review.

propositions.text: The RPD's dismissal of supporting evidence lacked transparency and failed to identify affidavits with striking similarities and unclear firsthand knowledge.
propositions.quote: the applicant had submitted on appeal that the RPD’s dismissal of this evidence lacked transparency because it did not identify the affidavits that bore striking similarities and about which it was unclear whether the deponents had first-hand knowledge of the matters described.

propositions.text: The statement that fraudulent documents are readily available in Pakistan was insufficient to dismiss the supporting evidence.
propositions.quote: The applicant had also submitted that the bald statement that fraudulent documents are readily available in Pakistan was an insufficient basis on which to dismiss the substantial body of supporting evidence he had provided.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the RPD's dismissal of supporting evidence lacked transparency and was insufficiently justified.

propositions.text: The RAD identified two affidavits as almost identical and unclear if affiants witnessed events described.
propositions.quote: In its decision, the RAD identified the two affidavits in question. It found that the similarities “are obvious as they are almost identical.” It also agreed with the RPD that it is unclear whether the affiants personally witnessed the events described in the affidavits.

propositions.text: The RAD erred by failing to consider the balance of the supporting documents.
propositions.quote: He argues, however, that the RAD fell into reviewable error by failing to consider the balance of the supporting documents.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found two affidavits nearly identical and unclear on firsthand knowledge; the applicant argues RAD failed to consider other documents.

propositions.text: The court disagrees that the RAD failed to consider the supporting documents.
propositions.quote: I do not agree.

propositions.text: The RAD reviewed supporting documents and found they did not overcome credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The RAD expressly states that it reviewed the applicant’s supporting documents and found that they did not overcome the significant credibility concerns that it had.

propositions.text: The RAD's brief reasons are sufficient given the applicant's general submissions.
propositions.quote: While the RAD could certainly have said more about why it reached this conclusion, its brief reasons are a sufficient response given how the applicant framed this ground of appeal.

propositions.text: Vavilov requires administrative decision makers to meaningfully account for central issues and concerns raised by parties.
propositions.quote: As Vavilov holds, the “principles of justification and transparency require that an administrative decision maker’s reasons meaningfully account for the central issues and concerns raised by the parties” (at para 127).

propositions.text: Absence of detailed submissions and reasons does not call RAD's reasonableness into question.
propositions.quote: In the absence of more detailed submissions from the applicant on this issue, the absence of more detailed reasons from the RAD does not call the reasonableness of its assessment of this issue into question.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD considered supporting documents sufficiently and the lack of detailed reasons does not undermine reasonableness.

propositions.text: The applicant did not argue it was unreasonable for RAD to find supporting evidence insufficient to overcome credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: the applicant has not even attempted to argue on review that it was not reasonably open to the RAD to conclude that the supporting evidence was insufficient to overcome its credibility concerns.

propositions.text: The applicant's argument is only that RAD failed to consider supporting evidence, which the court rejects.
propositions.quote: His argument is simply that the RAD erred by failing to consider the supporting evidence. As I have just explained, I am not persuaded that the RAD so erred.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the applicant did not argue unreasonableness of RAD's conclusion and rejects the claim RAD failed to consider evidence.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the application for judicial review will be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: No serious questions of general importance arise for certification under IRPA paragraph 74(d).
propositions.quote: The parties did not propose any serious questions of general importance for certification under paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA. I agree that no question arises.

propositions.text: Judgment: application for judicial review dismissed; no question of general importance stated.
propositions.quote: THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question of general importance is stated.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious questions of general importance and dismisses the application for judicial review.
